justice: A continuous sidewalk exists on the right side with a planted tree line, indicating some dedicated pedestrian space rather than fully vehicle-dominated allocation.
A long roadside guardrail/fence separates the sidewalk/edge area from the carriageway, which can improve orderly use but may also limit flexible crossing and access to destinations across the street.

The street space under the elevated structure is heavily allocated to motor traffic (multiple lanes, large truck presence), suggesting an imbalanced distribution of high-quality space compared with pedestrians/cyclists.
safety: A large heavy truck travels in the near lane under the elevated road, increasing crash severity risk for all users and heightening perceived danger for nearby non-motor users.

The elevated structure creates a darker underpass zone with strong light–shadow contrast, which can reduce driver visibility and increase conflict risk as vehicles transition between bright and shaded segments.

A physical barrier (guardrail) provides some protection for pedestrians along the right edge, but there is no clearly visible marked crosswalk or signalized crossing in the scene to manage conflicts at crossing points.
livability: Active ground-floor storefronts on the right (retail signage and entrances) support daily needs and street activity for multiple user types.
Street trees along the sidewalk provide a more human-scaled edge and can support a more pleasant everyday street experience compared to a fully hardscaped corridor.
The presence of an elevated roadway and high traffic volumes creates a strong infrastructural feel that can reduce social stay time and reduce the sense of neighborhood conviviality.
sustainability: Street trees provide environmental services (shade, air-quality benefits) and indicate some green infrastructure along the corridor.
The corridor appears highly car- and truck-oriented (multiple general traffic lanes, heavy vehicle dominance), which discourages low-carbon mode share.
No dedicated, clearly marked bicycle lane or protected cycling facility is visible, limiting practical modal shift to cycling.
aesthetics: The elevated roadway dominates the visual field and creates a heavy, gray overhead plane, reducing visual openness and streetscape appeal.
A consistent line of street trees adds greenery and improves visual quality along the right-hand side.
Building facades on the right appear utilitarian with dense signage and visible external fixtures (e.g., air-conditioning units), producing a cluttered streetscape character.
comfort: Thermal comfort is mixed: the elevated structure provides substantial shade to the roadway/edge areas, while the sidewalk area still relies mainly on tree shade that may be discontinuous.
Physical comfort for walking appears moderate: the sidewalk edge is present and buffered by a guardrail, but no benches or resting amenities are visible along the corridor.
Psychological comfort is reduced by proximity to fast-moving and heavy vehicles (truck nearby) and the enclosed feeling under the viaduct, which can feel noisy and stressful even with separation.
walkability: A separated pedestrian realm exists on the right with a tree-lined edge and a guardrail buffer, supporting basic walking continuity.
The under-viaduct environment can be unpleasant for pedestrians due to noise, darkness, and large-vehicle traffic, which reduces walking attractiveness.
Crossing convenience appears weak in the visible segment: the guardrail and absence of visible crosswalk markings suggest limited permeability for pedestrians needing to cross.
bikeability: No clearly delineated bike lane markings are visible on the carriageway, indicating low cycling priority in space allocation.
High exposure to heavy motor traffic (including a large truck) and the underpass environment significantly reduce perceived and actual cycling safety.
The roadside guardrail separates pedestrians from vehicles but does not provide a protected cycling track; cyclists would likely be forced to mix with traffic or ride on the sidewalk edge.
